method.residueTest: The state's legal-design memo, its track-registry projection and the national legal decision overlay for the jurisdiction are flattened into one string corpus. Every fragment of 30 normalised characters or more that the corpus already holds is deleted from the normalised text of the family's canonical PDF and participant-instructions.md. What survives in runs of 60 characters or more is what the packet adds to the design.
method.trapOne: Components a production field map declares -- in componentSet, in componentRoutes, and in the role list of each routeSelectionsMade instrument string -- that reports/rendered-artifacts.json does not carry. A declared but unrendered mandatory official form is an official-form-strategy change.
method.trapTwo: Each route's design destination kind against what the rendered packet is captioned to and who it addresses. A clerk destination is treated as a court destination, because the clerk is the court's filing office.
method.assertionTest: Every statutory citation, currency amount and duration on a platform-authored surface is checked for a source in the design corpus. On an official_pdf_fill family the PDF is the state's own form, so only participant-instructions.md is read as a platform assertion.
method.whatIsMeasuredAndWhatIsRead: Every figure in measurements is computed per family by this script. Bucket C and D determinations additionally rest on readings of the design records, carried in the generator's ADJUDICATIONS table with the exact quotation each rests on, because whether an assertion is substantive is a reading and not a computation.
method.fromTheOwnersRule: Fee, waiver, service and self-help text verbatim from the design record surfaces the approved design rather than adding to it. The same text with no source in the design is substantive. Where a family is genuinely ambiguous it is classified C, because wrongly claiming coverage attaches an approval to something nobody approved while wrongly withholding it costs only a review.

designReleaseBlockers.question: Whether a charge dismissed after successful completion of a deferred disposition under 17-A M.R.S. ch. 67 subch. 4 is confidential criminal history record information under 16 M.R.S. § 703(2). This was checked against current official text and is NOT ESTABLISHED. Section 703(2) lists paragraphs A through L and none mentions a deferred disposition. The closest is paragraph G, which reaches a charge 'dismissed with prejudice by the court or dismissed with finality by a prosecutor outside a plea agreement'. Under 17-A M.R.S. § 1903 the State dismisses the charging instrument WITH PREJUDICE on compliance, which fits the first clause, but a deferred disposition arises from a written agreement between the defendant and the State, which arguably falls inside paragraph G's outside-a-plea-agreement carve-out. Section 1903 says nothing about confidentiality or sealing. No statute, State Bureau of Identification guidance, Judicial Branch page or Law Court decision resolves it. The packet therefore fails closed: it does not promise confidentiality on the strength of the deferred-disposition label, it tells the participant to verify what the Bureau record actually shows, and it routes the correction request only where the record is demonstrably inaccurate.

Whether court docket entries for confidential dispositions are publicly accessible in practice, and what if anything a participant can do about that. 16 M.R.S. § 708(3)(A) puts records of public judicial proceedings outside the Criminal History Record Information Act and leaves public access to Supreme Judicial Court rule or administrative order, and § 709(6) says § 709 does not reach court records. The packet says so plainly rather than implying the docket is cured.

Whether a chapter 310-A sealing order removes the case from Maine's public court record search. 15 M.R.S. § 2265 makes the conviction confidential criminal history record information and restricts dissemination by a criminal justice agency, and § 2264(6) makes the State Bureau of Identification amend its records. designReleaseBlockers.question: Whether the § 9-23-23 expungement of a conviction, where the person was sentenced at the time of the guilty plea, issues without the participant asking. The section's operative language is automatic in FORM — completion 'will result in the record of the criminal conviction or adjudication being expunged' — and it is the only expungement provision in the Mississippi scheme with no petition, application, fee, hearing, notice or waiting period. But it also does not direct any officer to enter or transmit an order, and does not say the record shall be expunged without further action. Whether an order in fact issues sua sponte is therefore local practice and is NOT ESTABLISHED. The packet fails closed by verifying with the clerk what was actually entered before concluding anything, and in practice a movant should expect to submit a proposed order.

Whether a pretrial intervention noncriminal disposition satisfies the predicate in § 99-15-123(3), which reaches 'any case in which an arrest was made, the person arrested was released and the case was dismissed or the charges were dropped or there was no disposition of such case'. A § 99-15-103 noncriminal disposition IS a dismissal, but the subsection's arrest-and-release phrasing describes a pre-intervention posture and neither section says in terms that a noncriminal disposition under subsection (1) is expungeable under subsection (3). The same textual gap affects the near-identical § 99-15-26(5) and § 99-19-71(4). The packet pleads the statutory category that matches the participant's actual record and routes an ambiguous docket to advice.

Whether the Miss. Code Ann. § 99-19-72 fee reaches a given petition. The section reads: 'A filing fee of One Hundred Fifty Dollars ($150.00) is hereby levied on each petition to expunge an offense under Section 99-19-71 to be collected by the circuit clerk', distributed $100 to the Judicial System Operation Fund, $40 to the District Attorneys Operation Fund and $10 retained by the circuit clerk. Last amended by Laws, 1st Ex. Sess. 2017, ch. 7, § 12; no enacted amendment through 2026. Two things remain unresolved on its face and are NOT resolved by construction here. First, the trigger is 'each petition to expunge AN OFFENSE under Section 99-19-71': a § 99-19-71(4) non-conviction petition is a petition under § 99-19-71 but is not a petition to expunge an offence, because there is no conviction, and the statute does not settle it either way. Second, the collection mechanism names the CIRCUIT CLERK, which does not map onto § 99-19-71(1) or (4) petitions filed in justice or municipal court. Sections 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6), 99-15-26, 63-11-30, 41-29-150 and 67-3-70 sit outside § 99-19-71 and the fee does not reach them by its terms; none of those sections specifies a fee of its own. The packet therefore publishes NO fee amount on any track and instructs the participant to confirm the filing fee, and any pauper's-affidavit route, with the clerk of the court before filing.

Local practice in the twenty-one circuit court districts other than the Fourth, and in every municipal and justice court, was not surveyed. Both the review and the Fourth District materials establish that districts maintain their own petition and order preferences and that some expect the district attorney to sign the order as approved as to form before the judge will sign. This is a scaling constraint rather than a legal one: the statutory mechanism is the same statewide, but the accepted document and the practical gate vary. Every Mississippi track therefore carries localFormOverride and a mandatory clerk-contact instruction.

The section is the integration of two 2019 acts under § 1-1-109 — Laws 2019 ch. 362 § 4 and Laws 2019 ch. 466 § 41, the Criminal Justice Reform Act — with no enacted amendment since. Subsection (1)(a) covers felony and misdemeanour cases in circuit or county court on a guilty plea entered on or after 1 July 2014, OTHER THAN crimes against the person, a crime of violence as defined in § 97-3-2, a violation of § 97-11-31, or crimes in which a person unlawfully takes, obtains or misappropriates funds received by or entrusted to the person by virtue of public office or employment; (1)(b) covers misdemeanours in justice or municipal court; (1)(c) covers misdemeanour domestic violence in any of the four courts. Whether a successful nonadjudication dismissal requires its own petition under § 99-15-26, qualifies independently under § 99-19-71(4) as a case that was dismissed, or permits either route. This is the routing question and it is unresolved. The packet fails closed by pleading § 99-15-26 alone on this track, never merging the two statutes, and never reproducing the archived Fourth District dual citation.

Last amended by Laws, 1st Ex. Sess. 2017, ch. 7, § 12; no enacted amendment through 2026. Two things remain unresolved on its face and are NOT resolved by construction here. First, the trigger is 'each petition to expunge AN OFFENSE under Section 99-19-71': a § 99-19-71(4) non-conviction petition is a petition under § 99-19-71 but is not a petition to expunge an offence, because there is no conviction, and the statute does not settle it either way. Second, the collection mechanism names the CIRCUIT CLERK, which does not map onto § 99-19-71(1) or (4) petitions filed in justice or municipal court. Sections 9-11-15(3), 21-23-7(6), 99-15-26, 63-11-30, 41-29-150 and 67-3-70 sit outside § 99-19-71 and the fee does not reach them by its terms; none of those sections specifies a fee of its own. The packet therefore publishes NO fee amount on any track and instructs the participant to confirm the filing fee, and any pauper's-affidavit route, with the clerk of the court before filing.

Local practice in the twenty-one circuit court districts other than the Fourth, and in every municipal and justice court, was not surveyed. Both the review and the Fourth District materials establish that districts maintain their own petition and order preferences and that some expect the district attorney to sign the order as approved as to form before the judge will sign. This is a scaling constraint rather than a legal one: the statutory mechanism is the same statewide, but the accepted document and the practical gate vary. Every Mississippi track therefore carries localFormOverride and a mandatory clerk-contact instruction.

Trafficking-survivor relief under Miss. Code Ann. § 97-3-54.6, as amended by 2026 HB 1546 effective 1 July 2026, is recorded here as a separately-listed matter and NOT as a tenth normalized source node, because neither the adopted Batch 2 memorandum nor the authoritative source crosswalk lists it among Mississippi's nine core adult slots. The enrolled text was read: new § 97-3-54.6(6) lets the sentencing court, at any time after a conviction or adjudication of delinquency of a misdemeanour or a felony not classified as a crime of violence under § 97-3-2, expunge on appropriate motion where it finds by a preponderance that participation in the offence occurred during the period the person was being trafficked and was the direct result of that trafficking; official documentation from a federal, state or local government agency creates a presumption but is not required; and new § 97-3-54.6(7)(b) provides that neither failing to raise the trafficking affirmative defence nor the court's finding on it affects the ability to file under subsection (6). This relief is broader and faster than ordinary § 99-19-71 conviction expungement, so screening for it belongs on every intake. Whether it becomes a normalized node requires an express crosswalk or memorandum instruction.

Whether a case 'passed to the file' or 'retired to the file' counts as a case in which there was 'no disposition' under § 99-19-71(4). Mississippi practice uses that phrasing and the statute does not address it. The packet fails closed: the participant is asked to copy the docket wording, and an ambiguous entry routes to advice rather than to a pleaded allegation.

Whether the ten days' written notice to the district attorney required by § 99-19-71(2)(b) applies outside the felony conviction subsection. On the enrolled text the requirement sits inside subsection (2), which governs felony conviction expungement, and subsection (4) contains no notice provision. The packet does not import the felony notice rule, and instead serves the prosecuting authority contemporaneously and tells the participant that local practice may expect more.

designReleaseBlockers.question: Whether a conviction arising from the same criminal episode as the offence being set aside counts as a disqualifying other conviction. The controlling review states that it does not, calls the same-episode rule the clearest treatment of any single doctrine in the series and directs that it be preserved in the engine. The enacted text of Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 349, read at the Oregon Legislature's own channel on 2026-08-06, reads the other way on its face: ORS 137.225(7)(a)(B) disqualifies a person convicted of any other offence within the applicable period "whether or not the other conviction is for conduct associated with the same criminal episode". The enacted text does carve out motor vehicle violations, unlawful possession of a controlled substance constituting a drug enforcement misdemeanour, and under ORS 137.225(7)(b) a single non-motor-vehicle violation; the Oregon Judicial Department's own packet describes the carve-out the same way, as "except traffic violations or a single violation offense", and does not mention same-episode convictions. Neither reading is adopted here and no eligibility statement is made where a second conviction from the same episode is in play.

The current Oregon State Police record-check fee. ORS 137.225(2)(d) as enacted leaves the figure to the department, capped at actual cost, so the review's reported figure of about $33 per conviction cannot be confirmed from the statute and the department's current schedule was not obtained. The statute does settle one thing the review did not have: where the department performs only one record check it may charge only one fee regardless of how many counties the person files in.

How far the 2025 monetary-obligations relief actually reaches. The controlling review describes Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 395 section 1 as a general rule that expired judgment remedies for monetary obligations in any judgment of conviction count as sentence completion. The enacted text read at the Oregon Legislature's own channel on 2026-08-06 is narrower in its operative first subsection: it expires the judgment remedies for a judgment entered in a municipal court or justice court for a pre-July 1, 2015 marijuana-possession offence under one ounce. Subsection (2) then applies the sentence-completion consequence to obligations that have expired "under subsection (1) of this section". Whether the consequence in subsection (2) reaches obligations that expire under ORS 18.194 generally, or only those expired by subsection (1), is the difference between a broad unlock and a marijuana-specific one.

Whether the categorical exclusion lists in ORS 137.225(5), (6) and (7)(a)(A) as enacted have been amended again since Oregon Laws 2025 chapter 349, and how the person-felony and person Class A misdemeanor definitions in the rules of the Oregon Criminal Justice Commission map to particular offences. The exclusion screen depends on a classification the participant cannot supply.

What the December 1, 2026 version of § 19.2-392.2 does to this track. Read at source on 2026-08-06, the later version replaces the subsection A gateway with any person 'arrested, charged, summonsed, or indicted' for an infraction, crime or civil offence who 'is not ultimately convicted, provided that no stipulation of facts sufficient to find guilt was entered or the court did not determine the facts sufficient to find guilt but deferred adjudication or disposition to a later date'. That codifies the Dotson limit in the statute, extends the route to infractions, and adds a sentence to subsection C permitting a single petition to cover multiple charges arising out of separate transactions or occurrences, which the current version does not allow. It also provides that unavailability of the arrest information alone is not a basis for refusing expungement, and requires an objecting Commonwealth's Attorney to state the basis. The packet must be rebuilt for that version before it takes effect.

designReleaseBlockers.question: Which published form is the operative § 61-11-26 misdemeanour petition. The Judiciary Court Forms index was read at source on 2026-08-06 and publishes exactly five expungement forms. SCA-C900, captioned 'Instructions for Expungement of Records Petition' and revised 04/01/2021, is a five-page document whose pages 2 to 5 are themselves a petition, verification and certificate of service. That embedded petition is materially stale: it requires the petitioner to have been 'between eighteen and twenty-six years of age', requires 'no prior or subsequent convictions other than minor traffic violations', recites 'W. Va. Code §61-11-26 (2009)', and cross-references the exclusion list to '§61-11-26(i)', all of which are features of the pre-2019 section. The section in force places exclusions at subsection (c) and imposes no age limit. SCA-C906 matches the current subsection (c) and (d) structure and carries the § 61-11-26a elections, and is therefore used here. The packet must not generate the SCA-C900 embedded petition. Whether the Judiciary intends SCA-C900 to remain published in that form is not established.

The SCA-C900 instruction sheet, revised 04/01/2021, tells the petitioner that after a notice of opposition they 'will then have ten (10) days of being served of such notice to reply', and cites § 61-11-26(e) as the opposition provision. Section 61-11-26 was read in full at source on 2026-08-06: opposition is at subsection (g), and subsection (g)(3) gives the petitioner 30 days after service of the opposition to reply. The packet states the statutory 30 days and flags the discrepancy, but which the circuits apply in practice is not established, and a participant who relies on the form's ten days would not be prejudiced while one who relies on thirty might be.
